A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ToolGen work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite appendix expansion and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original ToolGen retrieval, end-to-end agent, ablation, hallucination, and generalization results in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds instruction-following, model-scaling, cross-domain retrieval, and training-data-volume experiments.

M1.justification: Appendix F introduces ToolGen-Instruct, which mixes general instruction-following data with tool data at a 50:50 ratio during every training stage. This is a limited training adaptation; the original token representation, three-stage method, losses, inference procedure, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates tool retrieval and tool-using agents. v3 additionally trains with OpenHermes-2.5 and evaluates general capabilities on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, CommonsenseQA, HellaSwag, Winograde, and GSM8K, substantially broadening training and task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds a Long-Context LLM comparator described as GPT-4o. New Table 6 includes Llama-3 and Llama-3-Instruct controls for general-capability comparisons. The existing retrieval and end-to-end agent comparator sets are otherwise retained.

E3.justification: v3 adds three-shot general-task evaluation, Qwen2.5 experiments at 1.5B/3B/7B/14B, I1-only retrieval training followed by I2/I3 testing, and 10%/50% retrieval-data conditions. Its new GPT-4o baseline uses a restricted 2,000-tool prompt containing the ground-truth tools. These introduce substantial new experimental designs; the original main-benchmark settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining v1's ablations, v3 investigates general-capability loss and instruction-mixing mitigation, sensitivity to model size, memorization's contribution to cross-domain retrieval, and its importance with reduced retrieval data. Appendices F, H, and J substantially deepen the analysis of capability retention and generalization.

E5.justification: Both Table 4 captions report means from three evaluations, and the retry appendices retain the same fixed-seed discussion. v3 introduces no new run-count, confidence-interval, significance-testing, or uncertainty-reporting practice; its additional results are point estimates.

E6.justification: Original main-table scores and the relocated ablation/generalization tables are retained. v3 newly reports general-task averages of 26.94 for ToolGen and 67.40 for ToolGen-Instruct, agent SoPR of 58.84 for the new variant versus 53.28 for ToolGen, and additional scaling and generalization results. New Table 7 also repeats ToolGen's average SoWR as 51.54, inconsistent with 51.51 in retained Table 4.

T1.justification: Appendix E.2 adds a worked probabilistic argument about length bias in constrained semantic decoding, using competing 0.7/0.3 branches and probability-one suffixes. This is a limited addition to mathematical reasoning, presented informally rather than as a formal proof. Existing loss equations, trajectory definitions, and Algorithm 1 are unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about unifying retrieval and calling through tool tokens, three-stage training, scalability, and competitive performance. The new appendix evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v3 clarifies that generalization tools were covered during memorization but absent from later-stage training. Appendix B distinguishes manageable parameter changes from entirely new tools or substantially changed usage, which ToolGen cannot currently accommodate. Other additions interpret capability loss, instruction-mixing benefits, scaling limits, and semantic-decoding bias, substantially sharpening applicability and mechanism discussions.

D1.justification: v3 documents the OpenHermes-2.5 source and access link, its 50:50 mixing ratio across training stages, and the new model configurations. It also clarifies existing stage-specific tool exposure and completes the numeric-tokenization explanation. Original hardware, principal hyperparameters, data-conversion instructions, and code/data access remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion and citations for TPTU/TPTU-v2, inference scaling, RLHF, and Qwen2.5, plus illustrative prompt comparisons with Toolformer and ToolkenGPT. Its central positioning relative to generative retrieval and tool-token methods remains intact. Several additional bibliography entries duplicate previously cited works.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence are largely retained. v3 moves the feedback-based-agent discussion into Appendix A, reorganizes and expands the appendices, converts experimental-setup bullets into prose, and makes local explanatory and header edits. The scientific additions do not accompany an extensive rewrite of the existing paper.

P2.justification: v3 adds four experimental tables and two figures showing prior-work prompt examples and model-scaling curves. Table 1 gains a comparator row, Figure 3's explanatory caption material moves into the body, and the dataset-statistics table moves beside the data-conversion discussion. Existing figures and appendix tables are retained under revised numbering.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves generalization largely for future work and does not test whether tool training damages general language ability. v3 exposes that important failure and evaluates an instruction-mixing remedy on six benchmarks and agent tasks (Tables 6–7). Controlled memorization and scaling studies, together with explicit tool-exposure and maintenance limitations, substantially strengthen validation and interpretation. These gains outweigh minor reporting problems, including conflicting attribution of the long-context baseline and the repeated SoWR discrepancy, although uncertainty reporting remains limited.
